## Question 1: Probability and Conditional Probability

A university health clinic screens students for a respiratory virus at the start of winter term. From past data, 8% of students carry the virus at that time of year. The rapid test used by the clinic has the following properties:

- Among students who carry the virus, the test is positive 95% of the time.
- Among students who do not carry the virus, the test is positive 10% of the time.

**(a)**: A student is selected at random and tested. What is the probability that the test comes back positive?

\vspace{5cm}

**(b)**: A student tests positive. What is the probability that they actually carry the virus? 

\newpage


## Question 2: Probability Trees and Independence

A basketball team plays a two-game series against a rival. In each game, the team either wins or loses (no draws). The probability that they win the first game is 0.6. If they win the first game, the probability that they win the second game rises to 0.7 (confidence boost). If they lose the first game, the probability that they win the second game drops to 0.4.

**(a)**: What is the probability that the team wins both games?

\vspace{5cm}

**(b)**: What is the probability that the team wins exactly one of the two games?

\newpage


## Question 3: Expected Utility

A farmer must decide whether to plant Crop A or Crop B before knowing the weather. There are three possible weather outcomes with the following probabilities and profits (in thousands of dollars):

|          | Dry (Pr = 0.3) | Moderate (Pr = 0.5) | Wet (Pr = 0.2) |
|---------:|:--------------:|:-------------------:|:--------------:|
| Crop A   | 20             | 60                  | 50             |
| Crop B   | 50             | 40                  | 10             |

**(a)**: Which crop has higher expected monetary value? Show the calculation for each.

\vspace{4cm}

**(b)**: Does either crop dominate the other (strictly or weakly)? Explain briefly.

\vspace{4cm}

**(c)**: Now suppose the farmer currently has \$100,000 in savings and has a utility function $U(\text{total wealth}) = \sqrt{\text{total wealth in thousands}}$. So, for example, if the farmer plants Crop A and the weather is Dry, total wealth is \$120,000 and utility is $\sqrt{120}$. Which crop should the farmer plant according to expected utility?

\newpage

## Question 4: Strategic-Form Games

Consider the following two-player game, where payoffs are listed as (Row, Column):

|       | L      | C      | R      |
|------:|:------:|:------:|:------:|
| **T** | (3, 1) | (0, 4) | (2, 2) |
| **M** | (1, 3) | (3, 1) | (2, 3) |
| **B** | (2, 2) | (2, 2) | (1, 3) |

**(a)**: Does any strategy strictly dominate another for Row? Does any strategy strictly or weakly dominate another for Column? State all dominance relations you find, or explain why there are none.

\vspace{4cm}

**(b)**: Find all pure-strategy Nash equilibria. Use the best-response method and show your work.

\newpage

## Question 5: Dynamic Games and Backward Induction

Consider the following game in extensive form. Player 1 moves first, choosing **A** or **B**. Then Player 2 observes Player 1's choice and responds. If Player 1 chose A, Player 2 chooses **C** or **D**. If Player 1 chose B, Player 2 chooses **E** or **F**. If Player 2 chooses F, then Player 1 gets a second move, choosing **G** or **H**. Payoffs are (Player 1, Player 2):

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  every node/.style={font=\small},
  dot/.style={circle, fill=black, inner sep=1.5pt},
  payoff/.style={font=\small}
]
% Player 1 root
\node[circle, draw, inner sep=1.5pt, label=left:{\textbf{P1}}] (root) at (0,0) {};

% A branch
\node[dot, label=above left:{\textbf{P2}}] (p2a) at (3, 2) {};
\draw (root) -- node[above left] {$A$} (p2a);

\node[payoff] (ac) at (6, 3) {$(4,\, 3)$};
\node[payoff] (ad) at (6, 1) {$(1,\, 2)$};
\draw (p2a) -- node[above] {$C$} (ac);
\draw (p2a) -- node[below] {$D$} (ad);

% B branch
\node[dot, label=below left:{\textbf{P2}}] (p2b) at (3, -2) {};
\draw (root) -- node[below left] {$B$} (p2b);

\node[payoff] (be) at (6, -1) {$(3,\, 4)$};
\draw (p2b) -- node[above] {$E$} (be);

% F sub-branch
\node[dot, label=below left:{\textbf{P1}}] (p1b) at (6, -3) {};
\draw (p2b) -- node[below] {$F$} (p1b);

\node[payoff] (bg) at (9, -2) {$(6,\, 1)$};
\node[payoff] (bh) at (9, -4) {$(2,\, 5)$};
\draw (p1b) -- node[above] {$G$} (bg);
\draw (p1b) -- node[below] {$H$} (bh);
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

**(a)**: How many strategies does Player 1 have? List them. (Remember: a strategy specifies a choice at every decision node where that player moves, including nodes that may not be reached.)

\newpage

**(b)**: Solve this game using backward induction. State clearly what happens at each step and what the final outcome is.

\vspace{6cm}

**(c)**: Suppose Player 2 threatens to play D (rather than C) after A, hoping to pressure Player 1 into choosing B instead. Is this threat credible? Explain, using backward induction.

\newpage

## Question 6: Mixed Strategies

Consider the following game:

|              | Left   | Right  |
|-------------:|:------:|:------:|
| **Up**       | (2, 1) | (0, 3) |
| **Down**     | (0, 2) | (3, 0) |

This game has no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Find the mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. That is, find the probability with which Row plays Up and the probability with which Column plays Left such that neither player can improve their expected payoff.
